prompt: Let $A$ be a set and $R\subseteq A\times A$ a binary relation on $A$. Which conditions are necessary and sufficient for $R$ to be an equivalence relation?

answers.explanation: The relation groups elements into classes: every element is in its own class, and class membership is reversible and transitive.
These define a partial order. A nontrivial equivalence class violates antisymmetry.
Reflexivity is required. On a nonempty domain, this combination cannot be an equivalence relation.
Asymmetry forbids loops, contradicting reflexivity on a nonempty domain.
Transitivity is missing: on the set $A=\{1,2,3\}$, all loops and the two-way pairs between 1 and 2 and between 2 and 3 can be present while both pairs between 1 and 3 are absent.
Elements with no incident pairs may lack their required self-loop.
This defines a preorder; reversibility is not guaranteed.
Connexity additionally forces all elements into one class; equivalence relations may have several classes.
Antisymmetry restricts every equivalence class to a singleton, giving only equality.
Nonemptiness does not supply a loop for every element; one loop on a two-element domain is a counterexample.
